claims.text: Near-equiatomic multi-element nanoparticles with minimal atomic-size mismatch and a buffering element have enhanced structural and chemical stability at high temperatures.
Near-equiatomic multi-element mixing induces lattice distortion.
High configurational entropy in a near-equiatomic mixture promotes formation of a single solid-solution phase.
Lattice distortion elevates barriers for atomic diffusion and segregation.
An oxygen sublattice in a high-entropy oxide can function as a buffer layer.
A buffering sublattice accommodates local strain and relieves local mechanical stresses.
The combined effects of diffusion barriers and stress buffering inhibit phase separation, surface segregation, and service degradation.
Nanoparticles with minimal atomic-size mismatch and a buffering element will retain an essentially unchanged single-phase structure and uniform composition after high-temperature exposure.
Increasing atomic-size mismatch will cause greater phase separation, elemental segregation, or secondary-phase formation.
Removing the buffering element will cause greater phase separation, elemental segregation, or secondary-phase formation.
The proposed stability mechanism applies across catalytic temperatures of 773–1173 K and thermoelectric temperatures of 473–1923 K.
The stability relationship may fail when atomic-size mismatch exceeds a critical threshold.
Atmosphere-dependent degradation mechanisms such as surface oxidation can dominate over the proposed stabilization mechanism.
Multi-element solid solutions can exhibit random or uniform elemental occupation rather than macroscopic phase separation.

contradictions.description: Lattice distortion is presented as stabilizing because it raises diffusion barriers, but increasing atomic-size mismatch—which would ordinarily increase lattice distortion—is predicted to destabilize the particles. The hypothesis does not distinguish beneficial mixing-induced distortion from harmful mismatch-induced strain.
